notes.meaning: The seventh month began with a sacred gathering and a complete rest from daily labor. The day was marked by the loud blowing of trumpets, calling the people to worship and reflection. This holy day gave a spiritual start to the civil new year.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some Christians connect the Feast of Trumpets to the rapture, teaching that Christ will gather believers at the sound of a trumpet.

notes.meaning: The priests were to offer a bull, a ram, and seven young lambs as burnt offerings, completely dedicating them to God. Each animal was accompanied by a grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, showing thanks for God's provision. All the animals had to be without any defects.

A male goat was offered as a sin offering to make atonement, which means to cover and remove sin so God and His people are reconciled. This reminded the people that they could not approach God in worship without first dealing with their guilt.

These special holiday sacrifices did not replace the daily morning and evening offerings, nor the regular sacrifices for the new moon. Instead, they were added to the normal schedule. Special occasions of worship build on daily devotion rather than replacing it.

The tenth day of the month was the Day of Atonement, a day set apart for complete rest and deep soul-searching. The command to humble themselves meant fasting and turning away from ordinary pleasures in sorrow for their sins. It was the only national fast required by the law of Moses.

On this solemn day, the people offered a burnt offering of one bull, one ram, and seven yearling lambs without defect. Each animal was presented with its proper portion of fine flour mixed with oil. These gifts were burned on the altar as a pleasing aroma acceptable to the Lord.

Along with the usual daily offerings and the special holiday burnt offering, another male goat was sacrificed for sin. This was in addition to the main sin offering described in the Day of Atonement ceremonies. It showed that even during their most sacred services, the people still needed forgiveness for shortcomings in their worship.

Five days after the Day of Atonement, the Israelites began the Feast of Tabernacles, a week of joy and celebration. They stopped their normal daily work on the first day to gather before God in praise. Having received forgiveness for sin, they could now rejoice fully in the Lord.

On the first day of the feast, thirteen bulls, two rams, and fourteen lambs were offered as burnt offerings. Each animal was presented with an exact measure of flour mixed with oil, along with drink offerings of wine. This was an enormous and joyful gift of praise for God's generous harvest.

In addition to the huge burnt offering and the regular daily sacrifices, one male goat was sacrificed as a sin offering. Even during times of great rejoicing, sin had to be acknowledged and cleansed. Joy in God's presence always rests upon His pardoning mercy.

On the second day of the feast, twelve bulls were sacrificed, which was one fewer than the day before, along with two rams and fourteen lambs. The required grain and drink offerings accompanied each animal, and a male goat was offered for sin. The daily morning and evening sacrifices continued without interruption.

The third day followed the same pattern, but the number of bulls decreased to eleven. The rams, lambs, grain, and drink offerings remained constant according to God's exact instructions. A sin offering was presented again to maintain holy fellowship with God.

On the fourth day, ten bulls were offered, alongside the two rams and fourteen lambs. Each sacrifice was given with its prescribed grain and liquid portions, plus the goat for a sin offering. God's people faithfully continued their worship as commanded.

On the fifth day, the number of bulls was reduced to nine, while the rest of the sacrifices remained unchanged. The people gave thanks for God's care during their wilderness journeys and for the abundance of the land. Each day brought renewed praise along with prayers for forgiveness.

On the sixth day, eight bulls were sacrificed with the two rams, fourteen lambs, and the goat for a sin offering. Every animal was offered with its proper grain and drink offering. God's worshippers kept up their sacred duties through the entire week.

On the seventh day, seven bulls were offered, bringing the total number of bulls sacrificed over the week to seventy. The rams, lambs, grain, wine, and sin offering were presented just as on the previous days. The number seven highlighted the complete and holy nature of the covenant blessings God had given them.

An eighth day was added to close the celebration, calling the people together for a solemn assembly. On this day, all regular work stopped once again so the congregation could worship. It formed a holy conclusion to the entire autumn festival season.

The offerings on the eighth day dropped sharply to just one bull, one ram, and seven lambs, along with a goat for sin. These were the exact same numbers commanded for the start of the month and the Day of Atonement. The smaller number taught the people that acceptance with God does not depend on the sheer quantity of sacrifices, but on His mercy.

All these sacrifices were national requirements for the regular feast days and fasts throughout the year. They did not take the place of personal gifts, such as promises made to God or freewill offerings brought out of love. Public worship and private devotion were meant to flourish side by side.

Moses carefully explained all of God's commands to the people of Israel just as he had received them. He was a faithful servant who made sure the nation understood how God desired to be honored. This established a clear and lasting pattern for Israel's worship in the Promised Land.
